extracted.intended_audience: early-career newspaper reporters assigned to the police/accident beat (city/police reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical reporting and ethical/style standards for covering crime and accidents on the police beat, including story structure, source-attribution, verification, office policy, and scene priorities. Focuses on how to write fair, accurate, non-sensational copy and how to handle chaotic accident scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique of fairness — six-block story structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Alter the story structure so the accused's version, however shorter, is presented as prominently as the police account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure: Block 1: Name of person arrested, statement of charge. Block 2: Circumstances of arrest (how/where). Block 3: One-paragraph summary of the police version. Block 4: One-paragraph summary of the person's defense. Block 5: Expansion of Block 3. Block 6: Expansion of Block 4. The proximity of Blocks 3 and 4 signals early that there is a defense and helps readers withhold judgment; it also allows the headline writer to use the defense without 'writing a head from the bottom of a story.' Even if the police account is expanded at length, the early defense summary gives readers an opportunity to see 'another side.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in naming persons mentioned by victims
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not name the person the victim mentions until a warrant is taken out, unless that person already is on the 'wanted' list and the crime is one of a series.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Victim certainty may be mistaken; reporters should refrain from repeating victim identifications as fact and should wait for official corroboration (warrant or official status) before printing names suggested by victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling confessions and 'the third degree'
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to confessions as 'purported' until you have seen them and know the circumstances under which they were obtained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of coerced confessions obtained by prolonged or illegal questioning; such confessions can be overturned in court. If a reporter contemplates inveighing against police interrogation practices, consult the managing editor — policy decisions are better discussed with senior editors. Treat confessions skeptically until verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid humor and careless inferences in police news
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor and inferences are always dangerous in police reporting; they can ridicule law enforcement or damage individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not lampoon officers or suspects casually — e.g., making fun of a rookie's mishap may hurt community relations and the individual's reputation. Avoid speculative inferences (e.g., implying a 'shake-up' where the chief says 'routine transfer') unless backed by evidence; premature interpretation can be proven wrong and embarrass the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and follow office policy on suppression and naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Each newspaper has specific preferences (do's and don'ts) — learn how office policy affects police beat coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common office policies include: omitting names for drunkenness arrests (because names often aren't verified); differential treatment of spouse brawls vs. other fights; setting an age limit for naming juvenile cases; withholding suicide labels until coroner/medical examiner findings; and refusing suppression requests from prominent residents. These policies are often unwritten and passed informally; reporters must observe them faithfully and refer suppression requests to editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mercy toward the accused and their families — avoid exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit details about family members and avoid cruel or sensational descriptions of accused persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when a prominent lawyer or clergyman is charged, do not print long, prurient accounts about family members. Keep family references brief and avoid language that prejudges or humiliates the accused (e.g., calling someone a 'Don Juan' or 'hypocrite' before a court finding). Consider the harm publicity does, especially to dependents and non-involved relatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Alleged' is not a legal shield — attribute potentially libelous statements to direct sources
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Alleged,' used so freely by police reporters, has no slightest value as a protection against a possible libel suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a disparaging or potentially libelous statement must be used to make the story complete, ascribe it to a direct source (e.g., 'police declared') to show foundation other than gossip. Know libel laws rather than relying on 'alleged' as a touchstone; 'the alleged swindler' can have the same damaging legal effect as 'the swindler' in the eyes of the law unless properly attributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid weary phrasings and standardized journalese
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not overuse hackneyed words and phrases in police reporting (e.g., 'dragnet', 'grilled', 'public enemy no. 1', misuse of 'youth').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many police stories are written rapidly and repeat similar facts, reporters tend to reuse set phrasings until they are threadbare. Invest time to find synonyms and fresher expressions. Reserve softening words like 'youth' for genuine minors; do not label a 45-year-old as a 'youth.' Repetitive clichés distort reporting and dull readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not 'blow up' a story to keep it on page 1 — avoid sensational inflation
rubrics_metrics.description: Refrain from expanding or inventing angles solely to sustain a front‑page run; exaggeration harms accuracy and credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid spinning pipe-dream theories or linking unrelated arrests to a major crime to keep coverage alive. Instead use legitimate techniques to extend coverage: review the case history, recap facts previously mentioned only on the run, describe intensive police work, or compare with earlier similar crimes. These methods keep stories alive without exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give the police a chance — be patient and avoid pillorying officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not pillory an officer who refuses to explain every thought and action; recognize police need time to weave sparse threads into a pattern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate lack of arrests or public progress is not necessarily incompetence. Avoid writing copy that shames or pressures investigators into premature disclosure. Patience and diligence are required; the reporter's thirst for immediate action must not intoxicate judgment. When following up, include tie-ins to prior coverage to orient readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a tie-in with the first-day account in follow-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime follow stories must include a tie-in with the first-day account, immediately after the lead, to help readers who missed the opening installment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early in follow-ups provide several paragraphs summarizing the high spots of the original story; as days pass this tie-in can shrink to a sentence or a phrase (a label/tag). Such labels (even 'journalese' like 'green-hat murderer') help copy editors and readers locate the continuing installment and maintain continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accident-scene priorities — three immediate demands
rubrics_metrics.description: On arriving at an accident scene the reporter's first concerns are: (1) to spot a telephone; (2) to see whether the accident is worth calling a photographer; and (3) to get names (the casualty list).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locate a phone quickly — if the scene is remote, watch for which buildings have lines. Decide on photography promptly because smashed cars may be towed and photographers may be busy; notify the city editor so space can be saved. Collect names immediately so the city editor can assess the severity for copy allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide quickly whether the accident merits a photograph
rubrics_metrics.description: A wreck needs a photo only if it has unusual or outstanding circumstances (e.g., a newly gifted car to a youngster, an injury to a U.S. Senator, a rollover of four times without injuries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the accident is the usual mangled cars, photographs may be in disfavor unless an unusual human-interest or notable-person angle exists. Photographers may have other assignments; notify them early to catch the best shots before vehicles are removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of names — 'NAMES MUST BE RIGHT'
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever names are offered by police or suggested by registration plates or letters found, they must be checked scrupulously; misidentifying someone causes real harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phone the names to the office and verify (directory, registration, interviews). A wrong name in a front-page photo can cause an hour of agony for an innocent family; there is no excuse. If names cannot be verified conclusively, present them as 'tentative' and explain why (e.g., 'Police believe the driver was X because of letters found in a coat in the car'). Do not assume probabilities justify firm identification — e.g., wallets or coats may belong to someone else.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid panicky exaggeration on initial reports ('ambulance chasing')
rubrics_metrics.description: First reports of accidents are often panicky exaggerations; do not assume the worst until verified at the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A caller's 'half a dozen bodies, all over the road' may reduce to one cut hand. Reporters should not repeat inflated initial claims without verification. Remember the scene is chaotic — check facts before amplifying sensational claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene reporting: vividness vs. accuracy under adverse conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Going to the scene gives a more vivid story but also greater risk of inaccuracies because everyone is excited, some panicking, and police are occupied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amid the welter of an accident, obtain facts accurate 'up to and including the middle initials' through careful interviewing and verification. Watch for misstatements from well-meaning but mistaken sources (ambulance drivers, bystanders) and cross-check with official records before filing.
